C005.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work office work]

[PATH:empirical] A controlled field experiment comparing task completion times and error rates for knowledge workers performing deep-focus tasks (e.g., software development, writing) in dedicated home offices vs. open-plan offices, with objective productivity metrics (e.g., lines of code, words per hour, bug rates). — Directly tests the hypothesis under the specified scope by isolating the effect of environment on deep-focus tasks, controlling for confounds like interruptions and office quality.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of pre-2020 vs. post-2020 studies on remote work productivity, focusing on studies that measure self-reported and manager-rated productivity for tasks requiring concentration, with stratification by home office quality (dedicated vs. shared space). — Leverages existing data to assess temporal change (post-2020) and scope conditions, providing a broader evidence base than a single study.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey study using experience sampling methodology to capture real-time productivity and interruptions for remote workers with dedicated home offices, compared to matched office workers, over a 6-month period. — Captures ecological validity and temporal dynamics, addressing the 'deep focus and minimal interruptions' qualifier through repeated measures of context and output.

scope.domain: tasks requiring deep focus and minimal interruptions, when the remote worker has a dedicated, quiet home office

C006.subject: office work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: office work remote work]

[PATH:empirical] Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J., & Ying, Z. J. (2015). 'Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment.' Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(1), 165-218. — This randomized controlled trial at a Chinese travel agency compares productivity of office vs. remote work, providing direct empirical evidence relevant to the hypothesis, though it predates 2020 and may not fully capture collaboration-intensive tasks.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of team collaboration studies in organizational psychology (e.g., Allen, T. D., Golden, T. D., & Shockley, K. M. (2015). 'How Effective Is Telecommuting? Assessing the Status of Our Scientific Findings.' Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 16(2), 40-68). — This review synthesizes multiple studies on telecommuting productivity, with attention to task type and collaboration, offering a broad evidence base to evaluate the scope-limited hypothesis regarding tasks requiring immediate teamwork.

[PATH:empirical] Controlled field experiment comparing office and remote work on collaborative tasks (e.g., software development sprints or design thinking workshops) in an urban corporate setting during standard business hours, pre-2020. — A custom experiment would directly test the hypothesis within its specified temporal, geographic, and domain constraints, measuring productivity metrics like task completion time, quality, and team communication efficiency.

scope.domain: tasks requiring immediate collaboration and teamwork

C007.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work office work]

[PATH:empirical] A longitudinal field experiment comparing productivity metrics (e.g., task completion time, error rates) for collaborative problem-solving tasks in remote vs. office settings, with random assignment of knowledge workers in developed countries with high-speed internet. — Directly tests the causal claim under the specified scope and qualifiers, controlling for selection bias and measuring the specific collaborative tasks mentioned.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of post-pandemic studies (2021–present) on remote work productivity in high-tech, collaborative sectors (e.g., software development, R&D teams), focusing on studies that measure spontaneous problem-solving and rapid feedback loops. — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess the consistency and generalizability of the hypothesis across multiple contexts, identifying moderating factors like team size, task interdependence, and communication tool quality.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of communication latency and information loss in remote vs. co-located teams, using network theory or agent-based simulation to predict productivity differences for tasks requiring rapid feedback and spontaneous coordination. — Provides mechanistic understanding of why and under what conditions remote work might reduce productivity, generating testable predictions that can guide empirical research and refine the hypothesis.

scope.domain: collaborative tasks requiring spontaneous problem-solving and rapid feedback

qualifier.geographic: in developed countries with high-speed internet infrastructure

[PATH:empirical] Bloom, N., Han, R., & Liang, J. (2022). 'How a Chinese firm used a natural experiment to show that working from home works.' Quarterly Journal of Economics. — This natural experiment provides causal evidence on productivity effects of remote vs. office work for focused individual tasks, directly relevant to the hypothesis's scope and temporal qualifier.

[PATH:empirical] Gibbs, M., Mengel, F., & Siemroth, C. (2021). 'Work from home & productivity: Evidence from a software firm.' IZA Discussion Paper No. 14734. — Uses granular productivity data from a tech firm, offering insights into task-specific performance differences, which can confirm or refute the hypothesis for focused individual work in developed economies.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of post-2020 remote work studies (e.g., Choudhury, P., Foroughi, C., & Larson, B. (2021). 'Work-from-anywhere: The productivity effects of geographic flexibility.' Strategic Management Journal). — Synthesizes multiple empirical findings to assess overall productivity effects across contexts, helping resolve the disputed status by identifying conditional factors and effect sizes.

qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on developed economies
